claims.text: The starting material is compositionally homogeneous (La0.25Eu0.25Gd0.25Yb0.25)2(Zr0.75Ce0.25)2O7 with a single fluorite phase.
This rare-earth-zirconate ceramic can be fabricated by TBA-based gel casting.
Varying initial solid loading can produce porosities of approximately 67–82% and average pore sizes of approximately 0.8–1.6 μm.
The resulting material contains a uniform, micron-scale open pore network in a homogeneous fluorite matrix.
The micron-scale pore network enhances phonon scattering.
Engineered pores reduce the phonon mean free path.
Micron-scale pores hinder heat transfer and thereby lower room-temperature thermal conductivity.
Adding pore-size-distribution and porosity descriptors to a CALPHAD-guided framework will substantially improve identification of low-phonon-thermal-conductivity compositions.
Combining CALPHAD-derived phase stability with pore-size characterization yields a predictive relationship between porous morphology and low thermal conductivity.
Ceramics with the targeted pore architecture will achieve room-temperature thermal conductivity below 0.07 W/(m·K).
The pore-aware model will improve prediction accuracy by roughly 15% relative to conventional CALPHAD-only methods.
Conventional CALPHAD predictions and earlier measurements of similar systems lack explicit pore-architecture integration.
The model is applicable only when pore architectures can be precisely engineered and maintained.
Processing variability and uncontrolled pore-size-distribution deviations will reduce prediction accuracy.
The exact prediction improvement is sensitive to processing conditions and variability in pore formation.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome field says either failure to reduce conductivity or deviation from the expected pore structure would falsify the hypothesis, whereas the formal rule requires both failure to cross 0.07 W/(m·K) and failure of the pore–transport correlation.
Uncontrolled pore-structure deviations are treated as outside or limiting the model's applicability in the boundary field, but are also treated as a falsifying outcome in the predicted-outcome field.
